title: What you still ask

cards: A hand goes up at the back of a study circle, just as everyone is reaching for their shoes. One more question. The teacher sits back down.
A year of learning leaves a few of those behind: the verse that still puzzles, the ruling that never quite made sense, the question of why that nobody ever answered.
After a year of pillars, schools and chains of narrators, some questions got answered. Others only got sharper. Today is for the sharp ones, not to close them, but to keep them.
Questions are welcome here, and the texts themselves say why.

teach.h: THEY ASK THEE: QUESTIONS IN THE BOOK.
teach.b: First, the book is full of questions. More than once the Qur'an opens a passage with they ask thee, yas'alunaka, and then answers.
They ask about the new moons, about wine and gambling, about what to spend, about orphans, about the spirit. Real questions became part of the book. Second, even a prophet asked.
In the Qur'an, Ibrahim says, in paraphrase: my Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He is asked: do you not believe?

teach.h: IBRAHIM ASKS, SO HIS HEART CAN REST.
teach.b: Yes, he answers, but so that my heart may be at rest. A question isn't always doubt. Sometimes it's a heart wanting to settle.
Third, not asking can do harm. In a hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud, a man with a head wound is told by his companions that they know of no allowance for him to skip washing. He washes, and he dies.
When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, hears of it, he is angry with them and says, in paraphrase: why didn't they ask, when they didn't know?

teach.h: THE CURE FOR NOT KNOWING IS ASKING.
teach.b: The cure for not knowing is asking. The Qur'an says it too, in Pickthall's translation: "Ask the followers of the Remembrance if ye know not."

Fourth, asking has manners. The same book says, in paraphrase, don't ask about things that would only trouble you if they were made plain. So ask what you need, ask someone who knows, and ask in order to act.
In these texts, a question carried well is how learning keeps going.

how: Muslims bring their questions to an imam, a teacher or a scholar, in study circles at the mosque or one to one, and teachers often answer with the verse or hadith behind the answer.

games.q: what does “what you still ask” mean?
o: a question you should drop once the year of study ends
a doubt that shows your faith was never really strong
a question left open on purpose, so you keep on learning

games.q: what you still ask — tap the pairs.
p: asked so his heart could rest
the man with the head wound
ask the followers of the Remembrance

s: in the Qur'an, asking a question always means doubting
Ibrahim asks to see how the dead are given life, and says it is so his heart may be at rest.
the Qur'an records questions people brought, and answers them
passages open with "they ask thee": about the new moons, wine and gambling, orphans, the spirit.
the texts treat every question exactly the same way
the Qur'an also says not to ask about things that would only trouble you if made plain.

games.q: a friend is hurt and asks what the rule is for washing. you aren't sure. what do you do?
o: give the strictest answer you can think of.
say you don't know, and ask someone who does.
games.why: in the hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud, a wounded man was given a confident wrong answer and died. the Prophet said: why didn't they ask, when they didn't know?

practice: Let one question from this year rise, the one still standing after the others have gone quiet: a verse, a ruling, a practice, or something bigger.
Don't answer it; just find the words for it, the ones you'd want to read again next year. If you pray, you can set it before Allah in your own words, as a question still open.

wordCard.voice: What you still ask. The question this year left open, kept on purpose, because the texts make room for a question asked in order to learn. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: they ask thee; the words that open several of the Qur'an's answers.

carryVoice: Your line: keep asking. A question asked in order to learn is welcome. Tomorrow, the scholars.
